## Overview

`class OpenTEMPEST.UsersGuide.Overview`

*Overview of the modelling levels*

OpenTEMPEST builds large models from small ones. Every level is a model of its own that you can simulate, replace or reuse in a level above. Depending on the question, each level can be modelled in detail or with a proven simplification.

<table border="1" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="4">
<tr><th>Level</th><th>What it describes</th><th>Main models</th></tr>
<tr><td>1. Electrochemistry</td>
    <td>Voltage, reaction rates and reaction heat as a function of temperature, gas composition, pressure and
    current density. Lumped (ASR) or detailed (Butler-Volmer, ohmic and diffusion losses).</td>
    <td><a href="OpenTEMPEST_SOC_Electrochem.md">SOC.Electrochem</a></td></tr>
<tr><td>2. Cell (repeating unit)</td>
    <td>PEN (positive electrode, electrolyte, negative electrode), fuel and air channels and interconnects with
    mass, momentum and energy balances, discretised with finite volumes in 1D (co-flow) or 2D (cross-flow).</td>
    <td><a href="OpenTEMPEST_SOC_Cell.md">SOC.Cell</a></td></tr>
<tr><td>3. Stack</td>
    <td>Cells stacked between end plates with gas distribution and heat transfer to the surroundings, from a
    lumped 0D stack to stacks of 2D cells, with simplified stacks that resolve only a few cells in detail.</td>
    <td><a href="OpenTEMPEST_SOC_Stack.md">SOC.Stack</a></td></tr>
<tr><td>4. Module</td>
    <td>Several stacks in a shared thermal environment (examples in preparation).</td>
    <td><a href="OpenTEMPEST_SOC_MultiReactor.md">SOC.MultiReactor</a></td></tr>
<tr><td>5. System</td>
    <td>Stacks combined with balance of plant: heat exchangers, heaters, blowers, compressors, reformers,
    afterburners, downstream reactors, power electronics and controllers.</td>
    <td><a href="OpenTEMPEST_BOP.md">BOP</a>,
        <a href="OpenTEMPEST_Flow.md">Flow</a>,
        <a href="OpenTEMPEST_Blocks.md">Blocks</a></td></tr>
</table>

### How the levels are connected

A stack contains an array of cells `cell[Ncell]`, a cell contains a PEN, and the PEN contains one electrochemistry object per control volume `electrochem[N]`. The electrochemistry is a `replaceable model Electrochem`: you choose it once at the level you work on, and every level passes it down with `redeclare model Electrochem = Electrochem`. Gas media (`FCMedium`, `ACMedium`) and the flux interpolation scheme (`fluxInterp`) are passed down the same way.

Supporting packages:

- [Heat](OpenTEMPEST_Heat.md): 0D to 3D solids, conduction, convection, radiation and heat port adaptors.
- [Medium](OpenTEMPEST_Medium.md): ideal gas mixtures for fuel, air and exhaust.
- [Solid](OpenTEMPEST_Solid.md): temperature dependent properties of solid materials.
- [Units](OpenTEMPEST_Units.md) and [Enumerations](OpenTEMPEST_Enumerations.md): types used across the library.

## GettingStarted

`class OpenTEMPEST.UsersGuide.GettingStarted`

*Getting started: run a first simulation*

### Requirements

- Dymola (tested). OpenModelica works for many models but is not tested systematically yet.
- Modelica Standard Library 3.2.3.
- [ThermoPower](https://github.com/casella/ThermoPower) 3.1.

The migration to MSL 4.x without ThermoPower is in progress. See the [release notes](#releasenotes).

### First simulation

1. Load the Modelica Standard Library, ThermoPower and OpenTEMPEST (open their `package.mo` files).
2. Open [Examples.Stack.Stack1DTest](OpenTEMPEST_Examples_Stack.md#stack1dtest). It connects a stack of 1D co-flow cells to gas sources and sinks and to a current controlled power supply, and runs steam electrolysis with a stepwise current ramp.
3. Simulate it. The stop time and the solver are stored in the model.
4. Plot for example `stack.cell[3].pen.T` (PEN temperature along the cell), `stack.cell[3].pen.J` (current density) and `stack.cell[3].pen.Uop[1]` (cell voltage).

Faster alternatives are [Stack0DTest](OpenTEMPEST_Examples_Stack.md#stack0dtest) (lumped stack) and [SimplifiedStackTest](OpenTEMPEST_Examples_Stack.md#simplifiedstacktest) (a few detailed cells, the rest simplified).

### Next steps

The user workflows in the repository (`docs/UserWorkflows.md`) explain step by step how to build a cell test bench, choose or write an electrochemistry model, work with stack models, build a system model and extend the library in your own package. The Markdown library reference (`docs/library-reference`) lists every class with its parameters and connectors.

### Practical tips

- Keep your own models in your own package and use OpenTEMPEST models through modifiers, `extends` and `redeclare`, instead of editing the library.
- Start from zero current (`Jstart=0`) and ramp the current up once the temperatures have settled.
- Set the start values in the *Initialization* tab close to the expected operating point. Poor start values are the most common reason for a failed initialisation.
- Use a stiff solver such as Cvode or Dassl.

## Conventions

`class OpenTEMPEST.UsersGuide.Conventions`

*Conventions used in the library*

### Signs

- The current density `J` is positive in fuel cell (SOFC) mode and negative in electrolysis (SOEC) mode.
- Heat flows into a component through its heat ports are positive.
- Mass flow rates at a connector are positive when the gas flows into the component.

### Gas composition

The order of species follows the medium. The index into mass fractions `X` and mole fractions `y` depends on it:

<table border="1" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="4">
<tr><th>Medium</th><th>Species, in index order</th></tr>
<tr><td><a href="OpenTEMPEST_Medium_Fuel_CH4.md">Fuel_CH4</a></td><td>H2, CH4, CO2, CO, H2O, N2</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="OpenTEMPEST_Medium_Fuel_C3.md">Fuel_C3</a></td><td>H2, CH4, CO2, CO, H2O, N2, C3H8</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="OpenTEMPEST_Medium_Fuel_MethanolReactor.md">Fuel_MethanolReactor</a></td><td>H2, CH4, CO2, CO, H2O, N2, CH3OH</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="OpenTEMPEST_Medium_Air_Medium.md">Air_Medium</a></td><td>O2, N2</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="OpenTEMPEST_Medium_SimpleExhaust.md">SimpleExhaust</a></td><td>O2, CO2, H2O, N2</td></tr>
<tr><td><a href="OpenTEMPEST_Medium_FlueGas.md">FlueGas</a></td><td>O2, Ar, H2O, CO2, N2</td></tr>
</table>

### Geometry and discretisation

- `x` is the fuel flow direction, `y` the cell width (the air flow direction in cross-flow cells) and `z` the stacking direction.
- `lX`, `lY`, `lZ` are lengths in these directions; `N`, `nX`, `nY` are numbers of control volumes; `Ncell` is the number of cells in a stack.
- Abbreviations: PEN (positive electrode, electrolyte, negative electrode), FC (fuel channel), AC (air channel), IC (interconnect), ASR (area specific resistance), BoP (balance of plant).

### Units

All variables are in SI units. Correlations fitted in other units say so in their description, for example the ASR correlations in [SOC.Electrochem.ASR](OpenTEMPEST_SOC_Electrochem_ASR.md), which are written for Ohm.cm<sup>2</sup> but return Ohm.m<sup>2</sup>.

### Documentation

Every class and parameter has a short description string (sentence case, no full stop). Longer documentation is in the info text, with sections as `<h4>` headings. The rules are written down in `docs/DocumentationStyle.md` in the repository.

## ReleaseNotes

`class OpenTEMPEST.UsersGuide.ReleaseNotes`

*Release notes*

### Development version

- Uniform description strings for all classes and info texts following one style.
- User's guide in the library, user workflows and a Markdown library reference in the repository.
- Planned: migration to the Modelica Standard Library 4.x and own gas and heat interfaces, so that ThermoPower is no longer needed.

### Version 0.1.0

First public release of OpenTEMPEST, based on the Modelica Standard Library 3.2.3 and ThermoPower 3.1.

- Electrochemistry: lumped ASR and detailed Butler-Volmer models for steam, CO2 and co-electrolysis.
- Cells: 1D co-flow and 2D cross-flow cells, and a cross-flow cell with simplified 1D channels.
- Stacks: 0D, 1D and cross-flow stacks, and simplified stacks with a few detailed cells.
- Balance of plant: heat exchangers, heaters, blowers, compressors, reformers, afterburner, methanol synthesis and power electronics.
- Examples for the stack models.

## References

`class OpenTEMPEST.UsersGuide.References`

*Publications*

If you use OpenTEMPEST in your work, please cite the software ([doi:10.5281/zenodo.21771899](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21771899)) and the publication that describes the models you used.

- J. Hollmann et al. 2026. Improving low-load efficiency of marine SOFC powertrains by means of efficient module hot standby operation. *J. Electrochem. Soc.* 173, 124503. [doi:10.1149/1945-7111/ae7479](https://doi.org/10.1149/1945-7111/ae7479)
- R. Lorenz et al. 2025. Control concept for solid oxide electrolysis reactors to promote highly transient operation in modular plants. *Energy Convers. Manag. X* 28, 101236. [doi:10.1016/j.ecmx.2025.101236](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ecmx.2025.101236)
- F. Sedeqi et al. 2024. Solid oxide cell reactor model for transient and stationary electrochemical H2O and CO2 conversion process studies. *J. Electrochem. Soc.* 171, 074507. [doi:10.1149/1945-7111/ad5e01](https://doi.org/10.1149/1945-7111/ad5e01)
- M. Tomberg et al. 2023. Operation strategies for a flexible megawatt scale electrolysis system for synthesis gas and hydrogen production with direct air capture of carbon dioxide. *Sustainable Energy Fuels* 7(2), 471-484. [doi:10.1039/d2se01473d](https://doi.org/10.1039/d2se01473d)
- M. Tomberg et al. 2022. A new approach to modeling solid oxide cell reactors with multiple stacks for process system simulation. *J. Electrochem. Soc.* 169, 054530. [doi:10.1149/1945-7111/ac7009](https://doi.org/10.1149/1945-7111/ac7009)
- M. Tomberg et al. 2022. Operation of a solid oxide fuel cell reactor with multiple stacks in a pressured system with fuel gas recirculation. *Energy Technol.* 10. [doi:10.1002/ente.202101075](https://doi.org/10.1002/ente.202101075)
- S. Srikanth et al. 2018. Transient reversible solid oxide cell reactor operation: experimentally validated modeling and analysis. *Appl. Energy* 232, 473-488. [doi:10.1016/j.apenergy.2018.09.186](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.apenergy.2018.09.186)
